newsitem.title: USA: Stock market jumps on election results.
newsitem.headline: Stock market jumps on election results.

text.p: Stock prices jumped Wednesday, with the Dow Jones industrial average edging into record ground as Wall Street endorsed the outcome of the national elections that will take the country into the next century.
In the 50 minutes of trading, the Dow Jones was up a solid 35.04 points at 6,116.22, surpassing its record closing high of 6,094.23 set on Oct. 18.
Investors were happy with the re-election of President Clinton and Republicans winning the battle for control of Congress -- the status quo that the financial community had sought.
Bonds were steady, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond inching up to 6.60 from Tuesday's close of 6.59 percent after initially dropping to 6.57 percent -- the lowest since March 7.
The dollar was lower after an early rally drew profit-taking. In New York trading, the dollar slipped to 1.5175 marks from 1.5200 on Tuesday and to 113.80 yen from 114.25.

"Both Clinton and the Republicans keeping Congress is very positive for the stock market and the bond market and that Mr. Yeltsin survived his operation is also another big plus for global economies," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

Clinton swept to victory over Republican Bob Dole, riding an upbeat economy to win four more years in the White House. The win makes him the first Democrat to be re-elected president in more than 50 years.

"We ought to be able to keep the economy going," Labour Secretary Robert Reich said, looking ahead to Clinton's second term. He told Reuters Financial Television he saw no reason why the 5-1/2-year-old economic expansion cannot continue for another four years.
The stock market, hoping for the status-quo in Washington, threw an early celebration on Tuesday, with the Dow closing with a gain of 39.50 points.

Foreign stock markets were also happy with the outcome of the election. Tokyo's Nikkei index surged 399 points to end just below 21,000 and Hong Kong stocks stormed into record territory. In London, the FTSE 100 rose 6.5 to 3,927.

"This has really eliminated an uncertainty that has bothered the market," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "People are comfortable and grateful that the uncertainty is behind them."
Markets have enjoyed an environment of low inflation, strong economic growth and falling budget deficits under the stewardship of the present administration.

There had been concern that the Democrats, riding on Clinton's coattails, would retake control of Congress. But their failure to wrestle the House and Senate from the Republicans was seen as a big plus.
